# Conclusions

Major results: 

- working with current detectors, involvement in the LVK
    - GW250114 paper writing
    - improvements to data analysis pipelines: windowing factor
    - interfacing waveform models: TEOBResumS-DALí, and analyses done with it
- understanding and helping the problems we will have when doing PE with ET
    - waveform accuracy requirements (bluebook)
    - fast PE requirements
    - `mlgw_bns`, accurate fast surrogate
    - fast PE for massive BBH with DINGO
    - Fisher matrix limitations
- defining the science case for the LGWA
    - sky position and timing for early warning
    - chirp mass as a proxy for low-PN order effects, eccentricity, environmental effects and so forth
    - massive sources and horizons
- understanding and helping the problems we will have when doing PE with LGWA
    - understanding how the detector's operational principle relates to its science case
    - timing: dependence on what and where, and effect on sampling

This thesis summarizes several novel findings in gravitational wave science,
related to the detection and analysis of recent gravitational wave events and 
the preparation of data analysis techniques required for future detectors.

The author was part of the paper writing team for the GW250114 detection paper, 
published in Physical Review Letters [@abacGW250114TestingHawkings2025], whose
results are summarized in @sec-gw250114. 
This event set the current record for clarity, which allowed for precision 
analyses of the ringdown and inspiral.
